name: md5-optimisation (animetosho)
language: C++ (inline x86, ARM and ARM64 assembly headers)
baseline: OpenSSL v1.1.1h MD5 (itself hand-tuned x86 assembly), reading from `openssl speed md5` at 16 KB
workload: Single-buffer MD5 of long inputs, bytes per cycle normalised across seven x86 microarchitectures at locked frequency; the repo's hand-written x86 assembly variants versus a 'Standard' control schedule that the author says roughly equals OpenSSL.
claimed_speedup: README: 'beat OpenSSL's implementation by roughly 5% in the general case, and 23% for processors with AVX512 support'. Skylake: 4.734 cpb (GOpt, +5.35%), 4.546 cpb (NoLEA+GOpt, +9.70%), 4.051 cpb (AVX512, +23.11%); percentages are relative to the 'Standard' control, not to a printed OpenSSL number.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 11.0.0 x86-64 (no flags stated); OpenSSL v1.1.1h built statically, fastest of 3 runs
hardware: Merom, Haswell, Skylake-X, Airmont, K10, Piledriver, Jaguar (named by microarchitecture only, locked frequency); AVX512 variant measured on Skylake-X only
tradeoffs: x86 variants are microarchitecture sensitive: plain NoLEA is slower than the control on Merom, Piledriver and Jaguar, and the AVX512 variant needs AVX512 (the author says AMD Zen4's 2-cycle vector bit-rotate latency makes AVX512 undesirable there, so only Intel AVX512 benefits). Single-buffer MD5 only; ARM and ARM64 headers exist but no ARM numbers are published. MD5 is cryptographically broken.
caveats: The headline percentages are measured against the author's own 'Standard' control, which is assumed to match OpenSSL; no absolute OpenSSL cycles per byte are printed. Results appear as a chart image plus a percentage table; the README does not link the benchmark harness, and CPUs are named by microarchitecture rather than model. OpenSSL 1.1.1h dates from 2020 and the baseline is itself assembly, not compiler output, so there is no -O3 C reference comparison. Speedup of a few percent on most CPUs is within the range where microarchitecture changes the sign (plain NoLEA is negative on three of seven CPUs).
found_via: crates.io API search q='hand-written assembly' returned the fast-md5 crate, whose README credits this repo as the source of its assembly; opened the upstream repo page and README.md.

name: fast-md5
language: Rust (inline x86_64 and aarch64 assembly ported from animetosho/md5-optimisation)
baseline: RustCrypto md-5 crate (portable Rust), and AWS-LC MD5 called through aws-lc-sys
workload: Criterion one-shot MD5 throughput over 64 B to 1 MiB inputs against md-5 and aws-lc-sys, run with cargo bench.
claimed_speedup: README: 'On Apple Silicon (M-series) you should see fast-md5 come in roughly on par with AWS-LC and ~5-10% faster than RustCrypto across the 64 B - 1 MiB range.'
hardware: Apple Silicon (M-series), exact chip not stated
tradeoffs: Compression function is chosen at compile time (no runtime dispatch): x86_64 uses the NoLEA+GOpt schedule, aarch64 uses inline assembly, every other target uses portable Rust. no_std, no heap. MD5 is cryptographically broken; the crate targets legacy protocols.
caveats: The claim is written as an expectation ('you should see'), with no table, CPU model or compiler flags and no published x86_64 numbers. It is a port of animetosho/md5-optimisation, so it overlaps that entry (the assembly is public domain per the upstream author). AWS-LC's MD5 is itself assembly, so 'on par' is parity with another hand-written kernel. The RustCrypto baseline is portable Rust compiled by rustc, not C -O3.
found_via: crates.io API search q='hand-written assembly' / 'hand-written asm' (crate fast-md5, description 'Optimized MD5 with hand-written x86_64 and aarch64 assembly cores, plus a portable Rust fallback'); opened the repo page and raw README.md.

name: zeebo/blake3
language: Go (AVX2/SSE4.1/AVX-512/NEON/SVE2 assembly generated with avo, pure Go fallback)
baseline: The same library built without assembly (pure Go purego path), on amd64 and arm64; the Rust blake3 crate is compared only in SVG charts
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of buffers from 64 B to 1 MiB (Full Buffer, Incremental and Reset modes), assembly build versus No ASM build, plus Apple M4 NEON versus pure Go.
claimed_speedup: amd64 i7-6700K, 1024 KiB: assembly 262 us (4.00 GB/s) versus No ASM 883 us (595 MB/s), about 6.7x (derived from page data); Apple M4, 1024 KiB: NEON 459 us (2.29 GB/s) versus pure Go 1.00 ms (1.05 GB/s), about 2.2x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not stated; the 'No ASM' build is the pure Go path (no special flags stated)
hardware: Intel i7-6700K (no AVX-512; Rust limited to AVX2 above 8 KiB) and Apple M4
tradeoffs: Does its own internal buffering and no multithreading; small inputs are 3-4x slower than the Rust crate (about 100 ns absolute). Inputs of two chunks or fewer use the pure implementation on NEON. Pure Go fallback keeps other architectures working.
caveats: The assembly is generated through avo (programmatic assembly) rather than typed by hand. The author says he makes 'no attempt to get precise measurements (cpu throttling, noisy environment, etc.)'. Go version is not stated and the Rust comparison numbers exist only as SVG charts, so the C/Rust baseline cannot be quoted. The pure Go baseline is a scalar compile with no auto-vectorisation, so the ratio overstates the gain over a vectorising C compiler. The two README descriptions differ (GitHub About says AVX2 and SSE4.1; README lists AVX-512, SVE2 and NEON), and only AVX2 and NEON tables are given.
found_via: WebSearch restricted to pkg.go.dev ('Go package assembly AVX2 implementation vs pure Go benchmark speedup avo generated') surfaced Go BLAKE3 packages with AVX2 and SSE4.1 acceleration; opened github.com/zeebo/blake3 and raw README.md.

name: minio/highwayhash (Go assembly)
language: Go (assembly .s files for amd64 AVX2, arm64 and ppc64le, pure Go fallback)
baseline: The non-optimized native Go implementation in the same repo (ppc64le comparison); other Go hashes (SHA-256, SHA-1, MD5, SHA-512, Blake2b) in the cross-hash table
workload: HighwayHash 64/256-bit sum and write throughput on 16 B to 25 MB messages; ppc64le old (pure Go) versus new (assembly) at 8 KB.
claimed_speedup: README: 'The ppc64le accelerated version is roughly 10x faster compared to the non-optimized version': Write_8K 531.19 to 5566.41 MB/s (10.48x), Sum64_8K 9.58x, Sum256_8K 8.90x. Intel Core i7 3.1 GHz Sum256_1M 14928.71 MB/s; Graviton3 Sum256_1M 5279.79 MB/s; Skylake Xeon 8124M: HighwayHash 11986.98 MB/s versus SHA256_AVX512 3552.74, Blake2b 972.38, SHA1 950.64, MD5 684.18, SHA512 562.04, SHA256 383.07 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Go >= 1.11 supported; benchmark Go version and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 @ 3.1 GHz; AWS c7g.4xlarge Graviton3; Skylake Xeon Platinum 8124M @ 3.0 GHz; ppc64le CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Separate assembly per architecture (AVX2 on Intel, NEON/SVE on arm64, VSX on ppc64le) with a native Go fallback; AVX2-dependent algorithm design.
caveats: This is a Go port of Google's HighwayHash (google/highwayhash is already catalogued), so it may fold into that entry as a port. Only the ppc64le table has a pure Go baseline; the Intel and Graviton tables list absolute MB/s with no baseline, and the cross-hash comparison is against Go crypto implementations, not C. The README does not say whether the assembly is hand-written or generated, and does not name the Go version or the benchmark file for the Intel and ARM runs.
found_via: Not a registry hit: recalled while sweeping pkg.go.dev for Go assembly packages (queries 'avx2 assembly', 'neon assembly arm64'); opened github.com/minio/highwayhash, raw README.md and its commit list.
